coachMessages.text: Four discs forming the number '7': a diagonal arm, a horizontal arm, and a shared hinge. Find the two threat cells — they are both in the same column.

slides.infoProse:
<board instructions>Show a mid-game position (10–14 moves played) where Gray has exactly 4 discs arranged in a Figure-7 shape: three discs along a diagonal arm and two discs along a horizontal arm (sharing one disc at the hinge). The two Gray major threat cells should both be in the same column (the shared column of the diagonal and horizontal threats), on adjacent rows. Mark the four Gray Figure-7 discs with 'win' overlays ('Pattern discs') and both threat cells with 'tg' overlays ('Threat cells — same column'). Do not yet explain why having both threats in the same column matters. Legend: 'win' = The four Figure-7 discs, 'tg' = Both threat cells (note they share a column).</board instructions>

The Figure-7 is named for its visual shape: a diagonal arm and a horizontal arm sharing a hinge disc. The key property is structural — both threat cells land in the same column on adjacent rows. Find these two cells and count: they are one row apart, same column.

coachMessages.text: Watch what happens when your opponent blocks the lower threat cell. Their block is directly below your upper threat — it just activated it.

slides.infoProse:
<board instructions>Show the same Figure-7 position as slide 1, then show the result AFTER the opponent plays into the shared column, blocking the lower threat cell. The opponent's disc lands at the lower threat row. Because the two threat cells are on adjacent rows, the opponent's disc is now directly below the upper threat cell — the upper threat is now at the top of the column stack and immediately live. Mark the opponent's blocking disc with 'td' ('Blocks lower threat'), and mark the now-active upper threat cell with 'tg' ('Upper threat now fires!'). Legend: 'td' = Opponent's block (activates upper threat), 'tg' = Upper threat (now immediately live).</board instructions>

The adjacent-row property is what makes the Figure-7 a trap, not just a fork. When the opponent blocks the lower threat cell, their disc lands directly below the upper threat — making it the next available cell in the column. The block that saved one threat instantly activates the other. Your opponent cannot block both in one move because blocking the bottom one hands you the top.

coachMessages.text: What if both threat cells are already at the top of the stack? Then it is a direct fork — powerful, but the zugzwang trap mechanism doesn't apply.

slides.infoProse:
<board instructions>Show a position with the same 4-disc Figure-7 shape as slides 1–2, but now the shared column is almost full — both threat cells (adjacent rows) are already at or very near the current top of the stack (both immediately or near-immediately playable). This means the opponent faces two directly playable threats, not a staircase lock. Mark both threat cells with 'tg' (both immediately reachable). Add a visible indicator of the column height (e.g., show the stack of discs below the two threat cells). Legend: 'tg' = Both threats immediately reachable (direct fork, not a zugzwang trap).</board instructions>

When both threat cells are already at the top of the column stack, you have a direct double-threat (a fork from lesson 3) rather than a zugzwang trap. Your opponent still loses, but the mechanism is different: they face two threats they cannot both block in one move, rather than a self-defeating block sequence. A Figure-7 puzzle specifically requires at least one threat cell to be above the current stack — where the adjacent-row trap mechanism is what wins.

coachMessages.text: The diagonal can also run the other way. The '7' becomes a mirror image — same logic, different scanning direction. Don't miss it.

slides.infoProse:
<board instructions>Show a mid-game position where Gray has a Mirror-7 shape: the diagonal arm runs in the opposite direction from the canonical Figure-7 (descending left-to-right instead of ascending, or vice versa), causing the shared threat column to sit to the LEFT of the hinge rather than to the right. The two threat cells are still in the same shared column, adjacent rows. Mark the four Gray Mirror-7 discs with 'win' overlays and both threat cells with 'tg'. The visual emphasis should be on showing that the shape is a reflection — students who only learned the ascending-diagonal form need to recognise this variant. Legend: 'win' = Mirror-7 pattern discs, 'tg' = Both threat cells (shared column, adjacent rows — same logic).</board instructions>

The Figure-7 has a mirror image: the diagonal arm runs the other way, placing the shared threat column to the opposite side of the hinge. Structurally, the pattern is identical — two threats in the same column on adjacent rows. The only difference is the scanning direction. Players who memorise the canonical shape miss the Mirror-7 in games. Whenever you see a diagonal three-in-a-row, check both the right and left side for the horizontal arm.

socratic.goalPrompt: Gray has a Figure-7 pattern hidden in this position. Find the two threat cells and name the column they share.
socratic._boardInstructions: Show a mid-game position (10–14 discs) where Yellow has exactly five discs in a canonical Figure-7 shape: three on an ascending diagonal (col 1 row 0, col 2 row 1, col 3 row 2) and two on a horizontal arm at the same height (col 1 row 2, col 2 row 2), sharing the hinge at col 3 row 2. Both Yellow threat cells — the horizontal extension at col 4 row 2 and the diagonal extension at col 4 row 3 — land in col 4 on adjacent rows; keep col 4 empty so both threats are latent (above gravity), making this a zugzwang trap rather than a plain fork. Mark the five Figure-7 discs with 'win' overlays and both threat cells with 'tg' overlays. Add 5–7 Red discs for mid-game realism but do not introduce competing Red threats. The student must click col 4 to identify it as the column that holds both threat cells.
